newsitem.title: UK: Gold's collapse goes on, miners suffer.
newsitem.headline: Gold's collapse goes on, miners suffer.

text.p: A collapse in the gold market began to take its toll on the mining industry on Monday when one South African mine was shut because prices are so low.

Anxiety for the future of many other high-cost mines, and anger in the industry worldwide, were fuelled by fresh declines in the price that took gold to 12-year lows below $315 an ounce -- down more than $50 since January.

The latest slide was triggered last week by news that Australia's central bank had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves. On top of previous disposals by the Belgian and Dutch central banks, the disclosure stampeded already-jittery investors.
In London on Monday gold sank as low as $314.10 per ounce, down $10 from Friday's close, before recovering slightly to an official afternoon fixing at $318.00.
But analysts were wary of predicting a solid rebound.
"It would take a Martian to be bullish at this point," said Andy Smith who follows precious metals for Union Bank of Switzerland.
South Africa's East Rand Proprietary Mines said it would halt work at its Benoni Gold Mining Co Ltd and put it on a care and maintenance basis. East Rand is a unit of Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd

"It's very, very bad news. They are calling it down to below $300 (an ounce) and if it does go to that there will be only three, four or maybe five mines in South Africa..." said Leon Esterhuizen, analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.

The sale of 60 percent of the Reserve Bank of Australia's gold hoard sent an especially bearish signal to speculators because Australia is the third largest producer -- at 289 tonnes last year -- after South Africa and the United States.

Bullion dealers expected investor selling to step up this week as New York reopened after the U.S. Independence Day holiday last Friday, and gold futures on the Comex exchange were duly lower by almost $10 in early Monday trade.

"We have broken past 10-year support levels, and the technical outlook implies that the next major psychological support is above $300 which the market may try to test," analyst Jim Steel of Refco said in New York.
In industry reactions, Australian gold miners pressed the World Gold Council (WGC), a producer lobby group, to make a statement criticising the action of their country's central bank.

The WGC said the sale seemed to be motivated by narrow financial considerations and that "for a leading gold producer to take unnecessary actions that prejudice the well being of a key sector of its economy suggests a lack of sensitivity to the factors impacting the market".

WGC chief executive officer E. M. Hood said the weak price would put additional pressure on member companies, several of which were in the council's hardship category even before the latest price slide.
"We expect others to follow with prices at these levels," he said.

Yet some dealers see the market's likely downside target as far down as the 1985 low of $287.25, which they say could be reached shortly on fears that other central banks might unload some of around 35,000 tonnes of gold that are held by government institutions around the globe.
Gold sank back in 1985 in tandem with a collapse in the price of oil.

Bullion had tracked oil higher, to reach a record $850 an ounce early in 1980, at a time when it was seen as an investor refuge from the inflation that had been triggered by the OPEC oil "shocks" of the 1970s.

Stockbroker T. Hoare and Co's mining equities analyst, Roger Chaplin, calculates average total costs of mining gold are around $350 including head office, exploration, depreciation and financing charges.

He said forward sales hedging programmes had allowed the mines to lock in previous higher prices which would help them for now, but of the top 11 North American mining companies "five or six will be on the border at today's prices."
